title: Microsoft 365 MCP Servers: What They Are (2026 Guide)
summary: Microsoft 365 MCP is a permissions framework for Microsoft services. Determine which access tier your organization needs and evaluate the costs.
body_markdown:
## Over-permissioning risks in Microsoft 365 MCP


That gap is where the mistakes start. **A prompt-injected agent inherits everything the signed-in user can do, so every excess permission is reachable by whoever writes the injected text.** Five mistakes recur:


> **A prompt-injected agent inherits everything the signed-in user can do, so every excess permission is reachable by whoever writes the injected text.


- Broad Graph scopes such as Files.ReadWrite.All: let one hijacked request read or overwrite every file the user can reach.
- Unvetted community servers put code you haven't reviewed between the agent and your tenant.
- Stored tokens turn one leaked file into standing access that outlives the session.
- No logging means you can't say afterward what the agent touched.
- Open-ended agents on fixed processes hand judgment to a model where a script would do.


It works for every demo, which is why Files.ReadWrite.All is easy to grant. It also means an agent summarizing one SharePoint folder can edit all of them. Scope to the task, and ask what the smallest grant is that still lets the job finish.


An SDK hands an agent code to run, but it supplies no tenant, no role and no audit log, and that is how agents end up running blind inside a Microsoft 365 tenant.


For fixed, repeatable work, such as a trigger feeding a set approval, Activepieces offers a Microsoft 365 connector, a separate route from Microsoft's own MCP servers, and agents get least-privilege access of their own, with custom RBAC and control over which apps a team may connect deciding what they can reach, so each agent is limited to the apps and permissions it has been granted, and a team can only connect the apps an admin allows.


Each tool call is logged separately with its own input and output, which answers "what did the agent touch" call by call. MoneyGram and Moneypenny run it in production.


### Unvetted community servers and stored tokens


To gauge how much a server can do on your behalf, count its tools. Third-party servers expose far more tools than Microsoft's own. The community ms-graph-mcp lists[53 tools](https://github.com/okapi-ca/ms-365-admin-mcp-server) , so you have 53 actions to review before approving it.


MCP-Microsoft-Office lists 117, which makes a real review a project rather than an afternoon. A 365 admin server lists 674, and at that size nobody on your team will read every tool, so you're trusting the author rather than checking.


Stored tokens compound this. A refresh token sitting in a config file lets a compromised server act as the user long after they close the app. Prefer short-lived tokens, and keep them out of files the agent can read.


### When Microsoft 365 MCP is the wrong fit


If the process is "when an invoice arrives, file it and notify finance," a workflow with fixed steps needs only the permissions for those steps.


An open-ended agent needs the whole menu, because you can't predict which tool it will pick. Reserve agents for work where the path is unknown.


Together these point to one design question: what is the least this agent must be able to do?
